chapters.name: Chapter 1: From caring to a plan

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Picking an issue you can actually change
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Choose one local issue and describe it in one clear sentence.
This lesson builds toward: Thinking about your school or community, you will choose one local issue and describe it in one sentence with who is affected and who could fix it, picking an issue you can work on safely.
Social impact means making things better for other people. Activism means working for a change. You do not have to fix the whole world. A small, local problem you can see, like broken water fountains at school or litter at the bus stop, is easier to change and teaches you how change happens.
Ask: Who is affected? What would better look like? Who has the power to fix it, such as a principal, a club advisor, a school board or a city council?
An AI assistant can help you brainstorm: "I am 15. What are some small problems teens can help solve at a high school or in a neighborhood?" Then pick one that matters to you and that you can work on safely.
Words to know:
- Social impact: making things better for other people.
- Activism: working for a change in your school, community or the world.
- Decision-maker: a person or group with the power to make a change.
Try it now: Write your issue in one sentence, like "Our school has no recycling bins in the cafeteria, so cans go in the trash." Add who is affected and who could fix it.
You can now choose a local issue and say who it affects and who can change it.

options: Fixing the whole world at once
check.why: Activism means working for a change; social impact means making things better for others.

check.q: You care about many problems. Which is the best first choice?
options: Litter at your bus stop that you can see and help fix
A problem in a country you know nothing about
check.why: A small, local problem is easier to change and teaches you how change happens.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Researching with AI and checking every fact
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Use AI to start research, then confirm facts with trusted sources.
This lesson builds toward: Using an AI assistant and trusted sources, you will research your issue and check every fact, plus gather your own evidence, using only facts confirmed by an official site or a real person.
AI is a good starting point: "Explain why schools recycle and what usually stops them. Suggest questions I should ask my principal." But AI can be wrong or out of date, and it sometimes makes up numbers or sources. This is called a hallucination.
Every fact you plan to use in a message must be checked. Trusted sources include your school or district website, your city's official website, government sites (many end in .gov), and real people like a teacher, librarian or the office in charge.
Your own evidence counts too. Count the overflowing trash cans, take photos of the problem (not of people without permission), or run a short survey of classmates with a teacher's OK.
Step by step:
- Ask AI to explain the issue and suggest questions.
- Write down any facts you want to use.
- Check each fact on an official site or with a real person.
- Collect your own evidence: counts, photos of places, a short survey.
- Throw out any fact you cannot confirm.
Words to know:
- Hallucination: when AI writes something that sounds true but is made up.
- Evidence: facts or proof that support what you say.
- Survey: a short set of questions you ask many people.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant to explain your issue and give you three facts. Check each fact with a trusted source and mark it "confirmed" or "not confirmed". Then gather one piece of your own evidence.
You can now research an issue with AI and keep only the facts you confirmed with trusted sources.

check.q: Which is a trusted source for a school district rule?
options: An AI answer with no source
check.why: Official school, district, city and government sites are trusted sources.

check.q: You want photos to show the litter problem. What do you photograph?
options: The littered places, not people without permission
check.why: Photos of the problem are good evidence; do not photograph people without permission.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Planning one small action
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn your issue into one small action with a date, helpers and an adult supporter.
This lesson builds toward: Given your issue, you will plan one small action with a date, helpers, needed permissions and an adult supporter, with permission in place before you start.
Good actions are specific: a cleanup day, a recycling-bin proposal to the principal, a supply drive, a speech at a student council meeting. Pick one you can do in the next few weeks.
Ask AI: "Help me plan a one-hour park cleanup for 10 students. List supplies, safety rules, who to ask for permission and a simple timeline." Then check the plan with an adult.
Safety first: get permission from your school or the park's owner, have a parent, guardian or teacher involved, never go alone, and follow any rules about gloves, roads or trash.
Step by step:
- Choose one specific action.
- Ask AI for a checklist: supplies, steps, timeline, permissions.
- Pick a date and helpers.
- Ask a parent, guardian, teacher or advisor to support you.
- Get any permission you need before you start.
Words to know:
- Action plan: a list of what you will do, when, and who helps.
- Supporter: an adult who helps and checks your plan.
Try it now: Use an AI assistant to plan one small action for your issue. Write down the date, two helpers, the permission you need, and the adult who will support you.
You can now turn an issue into a safe, specific action plan with adult support.

options: It has a clear what, a date and who is helping
check.why: Specific actions say what you will do, when and with whom.

check.q: You plan a cleanup in a city park. What do you do before the day?
options: Get permission from the park's owner and have an adult involved
Post your home address for helpers
check.why: Safety first: get permission, involve an adult and never go alone.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Speaking up and spreading the word

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Writing a respectful message to a decision-maker
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI to draft a clear, respectful letter or email, then make it yours.
This lesson builds toward: Given your checked facts, you will write a short, respectful message to a decision-maker with a specific ask, rewritten in your own words and read by an adult before sending.
A strong message is short and polite: who you are (first name, grade, school or neighborhood), the problem in one sentence, one or two checked facts, a specific ask, and a thank you.
Ask AI: "Help me write a short, respectful email to my principal asking for recycling bins in the cafeteria. I am a 10th grader. Here are my facts: [your checked facts]. Keep it under 150 words." Then rewrite it in your own words and remove anything you did not check.
To find who to contact, look at your school or district website, or your city's official website. USA.gov has a page that links to federal, state and local elected officials. Have a parent, guardian or teacher read your message before you send it.
Step by step:
- Say who you are without private details beyond first name and grade.
- State the problem in one sentence.
- Add one or two checked facts.
- Make a specific ask and say thank you.
- Rewrite the AI draft in your own words and have an adult read it before sending.
Words to know:
- Specific ask: the exact thing you want the person to do.
- Elected official: a person voted into a job, like a city council member.
Official sources:
- USA.gov: Find your elected officials
Try it now: Use an AI assistant to draft a message to the decision-maker for your issue, using only your confirmed facts. Rewrite it in your own words and ask an adult to read it. Do not send it until they have.
You can now write a short, respectful, fact-checked message that asks a decision-maker for a specific change.

check.q: What is a "specific ask" in a message?
options: A clear request, like adding recycling bins in the cafeteria
check.why: A specific ask tells the decision-maker exactly what you want them to do.

check.q: AI's draft includes a number you never checked. What do you do?
options: Leave it in; it sounds good
Remove it or check it before sending
check.why: Rewrite the draft and remove anything you did not check.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Spreading the word safely
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Make a simple poster or post about your action and share it safely.
This lesson builds toward: When you share your action, you will create a poster or post that says what, when, where and why, and share it safely, from an approved account, with no private details and no personal attacks.
People join when the message is clear: what, when, where and why it matters. AI can help you write a short slogan or post, and free tools like Canva can help you make a poster. Check every date, time and place.
Stay safe online: post from a school club or family-approved account if you can, keep your full name, phone number and home address private, and do not share photos of other people without permission.
Some people will disagree. That is OK. Answer politely or not at all, and never post personal attacks. If someone threatens or harasses you, do not reply; save it, block, report and tell a trusted adult.
Step by step:
- Write what, when, where and why in a few words.
- Ask AI for three slogan ideas and pick or rewrite one.
- Make a poster or post and check every detail.
- Share from a club or family-approved account.
- Keep private details out and tell an adult about any threats.
Words to know:
- Slogan: a short, catchy phrase about your cause.
- Harassment: repeated mean or threatening messages.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant for three slogan ideas for your action. Pick one, make a simple poster or post with what, when, where and why, and have an adult check it before sharing.
You can now make a clear message about your cause and share it safely and respectfully.

check.q: What four things should a poster for your action tell people?
options: Your full name, phone, address and school
check.why: A clear message says what, when, where and why it matters.

check.q: Someone posts a mean comment calling you names. What do you do?
options: Reply politely or not at all, and tell an adult if it becomes a threat
check.why: Never post personal attacks; save, block, report and tell an adult about threats.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Responsible AI in activism, and your action plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Avoid misleading content and finish a one-page action plan.
This lesson builds toward: Before you share anything about your cause, you will check that it is true, checked and fair, label AI images, and write a one-page action plan, using no fake images or quotes of real people.
AI makes it easy to create fake images, fake quotes and fake news. Using them, even for a good cause, breaks trust and can spread lies. Never make fake photos or quotes of real people, and label any AI-generated image you use.
Before you share anything, ask: Is it true? Did I check it? Is it fair to the people involved? Would I be OK if the person I am writing about read it?
Now put it together on one page: the problem, two checked facts, one action with a date and helpers, your adult supporter, your message to a decision-maker, and how you will share it. Then reflect: what worked, and what would you do next?
Step by step:
- Check every image and quote is real or clearly labeled as AI.
- Ask: is it true, checked and fair?
- Write your one-page action plan.
- Attach your message and sharing plan.
- After your action, write what worked and what is next.
Words to know:
- Misinformation: false information, shared by mistake or on purpose.
- Label: a note that says something was made with AI.
Try it now: Final task: write your one-page action plan with the problem, two checked facts, one action with a date and helpers, your adult supporter, your rewritten message to a decision-maker, and your plan to share it safely.
You can now use AI responsibly to plan, speak up and share a small action that makes a real difference.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Clear problem The problem is vague or too big to work on. The problem in one sentence, with who is affected and who could fix it. Also says what better would look like. Checked facts Facts are unchecked or come only from AI. Two facts confirmed with trusted sources, and the sources are named. Also includes the learner's own evidence, such as a count or a survey. Action and safety No date, helpers or adult supporter, or no permission. One small action with a date, helpers, an adult supporter and the permission needed. Includes a short safety checklist for the day. Message to a decision-maker The message is rude, vague or uses unchecked facts. A short, respectful message with the problem, checked facts, a specific ask and a thank you, in the learner's own words. An adult has read it, and it names the right person to contact. Safe and honest sharing The sharing plan has private details, fake images or unlabeled AI content. A plan to share from an approved account with no private details, and any AI image labeled. Also says how the learner will respond to disagreement. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

options: A label on an AI image
False information shared by mistake or on purpose
check.why: Misinformation is false information, and AI makes it easy to create.

check.q: A made-up quote from a local leader would help your cause go viral. What do you do?
options: Do not use it; fake quotes break trust and spread lies
Use it but blur the name
Ask AI to make it sound real
check.why: Fake quotes or photos of real people break trust, even for a good cause.
